title: Assam Flood Death Toll Hits 85 as Waters Recede Across Upper Assam
excerpt: Three more deaths push toll higher even as affected population drops sharply to 1.35 lakh from a peak of 10 lakh, with floodwaters receding across Sivasagar and Charaideo.
body:
• Three more flood-related deaths take Assam's toll to 85 since a July 19 cloudburst triggered the worst floods in years across Upper Assam
  • Affected population has declined sharply from a peak of nearly 10 lakh to 1.35 lakh as floodwaters recede across Sivasagar and Charaideo
  • Over 45,000 hectares of cropland submerged and thousands of livestock lost; state government raises ex gratia to ₹9 lakh per deceased family

Three more people have died in flood-related incidents in Assam, pushing the death toll to 85 since a devastating cloudburst on July 19 triggered what has become one of the state's worst flood disasters in recent years. The number of affected people, however, has dropped sharply to 1.35 lakh as floodwaters continue to recede across the worst-hit districts of Upper Assam.

At its peak in late July, the floods had affected nearly 10 lakh people across 16 districts, with Sivasagar, Charaideo, Jorhat, and Golaghat bearing the brunt of the deluge. The steady decline in affected numbers — from 4.45 lakh on July 28 to 3.32 lakh by July 29 and now 1.35 lakh — signals a gradual return to normalcy, though the human cost continues to mount.

Context

The crisis began when a cloudburst struck Mon district in neighbouring Nagaland on July 19, sending torrents of water down the hill-fed tributaries of the Brahmaputra. The Dikhow, Disang, Dhansiri, and Jhanji rivers swelled rapidly, breaching embankments and inundating hundreds of villages across Upper Assam within hours.

Environmental experts attributed the scale of the disaster to a compound flash flood event rather than a typical Brahmaputra overflow. Foothill catchments in Nagaland recorded rainfall up to 493% above seasonal norms over a 48-hour window, according to the India Meteorological Department. Years of deforestation and unregulated mining in upstream hill regions had reduced riverbed capacity through heavy siltation, worsening the impact downstream.

"The situation has improved slightly, but we still have not been able to reach around 20 per cent of the affected people."

— Himanta Biswa Sarma, Chief Minister of Assam

The death toll climbed steeply in the first week — from 31 on July 22 to 47 by July 24, then 66 by July 26 — before slowing as rescue operations reached cut-off areas. The toll reached 75 on July 29 after seven deaths were reported in a single day from Nazira revenue circle in Sivasagar district, The Hindu Business Line reported.

Impact

The agricultural damage has been staggering. Over 45,000 hectares of cropland remain submerged, devastating livelihoods in a region heavily dependent on farming. More than 2.5 lakh domestic animals have been affected, with over 26,000 washed away or killed.

At the peak of the crisis, 872 villages across 44 revenue circles were underwater. Floodwaters breached six major embankments, damaged 33 roads, and collapsed bridge infrastructure in Golaghat, severing key transport links. The Northeast Frontier Railway was forced to cancel or divert several express services after tracks between Mariani and Simaluguri were submerged.

Charaideo was the worst-hit district with up to 1.88 lakh people affected at peak, followed by Sivasagar at 1.44 lakh and Jorhat at over 1.26 lakh. Relief camps housed over 32,000 displaced people at their busiest, with the Indian Army, Air Force, NDRF, and SDRF conducting round-the-clock rescue operations using boats and helicopters.

The state government increased ex gratia compensation for the families of the deceased to ₹9 lakh each, up from ₹4 lakh, and relaxed norms for availing the payment. A Gurdwara in Sivasagar became a lifeline for hundreds of displaced families, with Sikh volunteers providing shelter, food, and essential services.

What's Next

While the immediate crisis is easing, the recovery ahead is daunting. Thick layers of silt deposited across farmland and residential areas will take weeks to clear. Power outages persist in several pockets, and mud-clogged roads continue to hamper connectivity. Health officials have warned of disease outbreaks — including dengue, malaria, and diarrhoeal illnesses — from stagnant floodwater and contaminated drinking sources in overcrowded relief camps.

A central government team has assessed flood damage in the state, and Prime Minister Narendra Modi has spoken with Chief Minister Sarma, assuring all possible support for relief and rehabilitation. For the Indian diaspora, particularly those with family in Assam's flood-prone Brahmaputra Valley, the receding waters bring relief but the scale of agricultural and infrastructure damage means the economic fallout will linger well beyond the monsoon season.

Assam faces catastrophic flooding nearly every monsoon, but the 2026 disaster — driven by extreme upstream rainfall and degraded catchments — has renewed calls for a comprehensive flood management authority for the northeast, an idea the central government has floated but not yet acted on.
nri_angle: Indians abroad with family in Assam's Brahmaputra Valley face lingering economic fallout from massive agricultural and infrastructure damage even as floodwaters recede.
author: Diaspora Desk
